urban-runoff-s1.title: Three ways to reduce urban runoff

urban-runoff-s2.title: Runoff from four parking lot designs

table.caption: Runoff measured from four test parking lots of 1,000 m² each during the same 30-mm storm (invented data for practice)
rows: Ordinary asphalt draining to a rain garden

options: A planted low spot that soaks up runoff
A greenhouse where the plants are watered with rain
A roof covered with soil and plants
A tank that stores rain for watering lawns

why.correct: A rain garden is a shallow, planted basin that takes runoff from roofs or pavement.
options: Right: a planted basin that soaks up runoff.
A greenhouse is not a runoff control.
That is a green roof.
That is a rain barrel or cistern.

items.q: How does permeable pavement reduce flooding?
options: Rain passes through into gravel and soil, so less runs off
It is darker, so rain evaporates from it before it can run off
It slopes toward the storm drains, so water leaves faster
It is smoother, so water flows off it more quickly

why.correct: Water drains through the pavement into the ground instead of running across it.
options: Right: water passes through and soaks in.
Evaporation is not how it works.
Sending water to drains faster is ordinary pavement.
Faster runoff makes flooding worse.

items.q: Besides holding rain, which benefit does a green roof provide?
options: It cools the building and the air around it
It makes the roof lighter, so the building costs less
It sends rain to the storm drain faster
It raises the temperature of the city in summer

why.correct: Plants and soil shade the roof and cool by transpiration.
options: Right: cooling through shade and transpiration.
Green roofs are heavier, not lighter.
They slow rain, not speed it.
They cool the city.

items.q: Which is a drawback of permeable pavement?
options: Sediment can clog its pores unless it is cleaned
It increases runoff compared with ordinary pavement
It is unsuitable for parking lots or sidewalks
It makes groundwater recharge lower than before

why.correct: Fine dirt fills the pores over time; vacuum sweeping keeps it working.
options: Right: clogging and maintenance.
It reduces runoff.
It is widely used for parking lots and sidewalks.
It increases recharge.

items.q: A city wants to reduce runoff but has little open land. Which strategy fits best?
options: Green roofs on large flat buildings already in the city
A large new detention pond on farmland at the edge of the county
Wider streets with more storm drains along each block
New parking lots of ordinary asphalt near each school

why.correct: Roofs are a big share of city surface, and greening them needs no new land.
options: Right: it uses existing roof space.
The question says land is scarce; and a pond far away does not help the city's streets.
Wider streets add impervious surface.
Ordinary asphalt adds runoff.

items.q: Why can building taller apartment buildings near transit reduce runoff for a city as a whole?
options: People live on less land, with fewer roads and parking lots
Tall buildings soak up rain through their walls, so less reaches the ground
Tall buildings block rain from falling on the streets below them
Transit lines are made of permeable pavement, so runoff soaks in

why.correct: Building up instead of out, and relying on transit, covers less land with roofs, roads and parking.
options: Right: less paved land per person.
Walls do not soak up rain.
Buildings do not block rain from a whole area.
Transit is not defined by its pavement.

items.q: A roof measures 120 m². How many liters of water fall on it in a 15-mm rain? (1 m³ = 1,000 L)

mistakes.why: 1.8 is in cubic meters. Multiply by 1,000 to change cubic meters to liters.
15 mm is 0.015 m, not 0.15 m: there are 1,000 mm in a meter.

items.q: A school's parking lot floods a nearby street after every storm. Propose a solution for the school and explain how it works.

why.correct: A solution fitted to one parking lot, with how it works: replace the asphalt with permeable pavers, which let rain drain through into gravel and soil, so less water runs onto the street.

solution.label: Solution
options: replace the asphalt with permeable pavers
add more storm drains on the street
repave the lot with new ordinary asphalt

why.1: More drains move water faster but do not reduce runoff from the lot.
why.2: New ordinary asphalt sheds the same runoff.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: lets rain drain through into gravel and soil below
sends rain to the street faster
makes the rain evaporate before it lands

why.1: That is what the school wants to stop.
why.2: Pavers do not make rain evaporate.

effect.label: Result
options: less water runs onto the street and it floods less
more water runs onto the street
the street floods for longer

specific.model: The school could replace the asphalt with permeable pavers, which let rain drain through into gravel and soil below. As a result less water runs onto the street, so it floods less.

items.q: In the diagram, where does the water from the downspout go?
options: Into the rain garden, where it soaks in
Onto the ordinary pavement and into the storm drain
Back up onto the green roof to water the plants
Through the permeable pavement into the gravel

why.correct: The downspout arrow points into the rain garden, and dashed arrows show water soaking in.
options: Right: into the rain garden.
The storm drain gets water from the ordinary pavement.
Water does not flow back up to the roof.
The permeable pavement is next to the garden, but the downspout feeds the garden.

items.q: What do the three methods in the diagram have in common that ordinary pavement lacks?
options: Each lets water soak in or holds it for a while
Each sends water sideways to the storm drain more quickly
Each is darker than ordinary pavement, so rain dries faster
Each collects water in tanks to be pumped back to the river

why.correct: Dashed arrows show water soaking into the ground beneath each method; ordinary pavement sends it sideways to the drain.
options: Right: water soaks in or is held.
That describes ordinary pavement.
Color is not the point of these methods.
No tanks or pumps are shown.

items.q: A neighborhood above a river installs all three methods. Which change in the river is most likely?
options: Lower flood peaks and steadier flow between storms
Higher, faster flood peaks after storms and less flow between storms
No change in flood peaks, but warmer water after storms
More sediment and oil carried into the river by each storm

why.correct: Less runoff lowers flood peaks; more recharge feeds the river between storms.
options: Right: lower peaks, steadier base flow.
That is the effect of paving, not of these methods.
Less runoff lowers peaks.
Soil and plants trap sediment and oil.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in runoff from the ordinary asphalt lot to the permeable paver lot, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, the 27 m³ from ordinary asphalt.
Subtract old from new: (6 - 27). Runoff fell, so the change is negative.
-21 m³ is the change in runoff. Divide by 27 and multiply by 100.
That is the change from pavers back to asphalt. Start from asphalt.

items.q: The storm dropped 30 mm of rain on each 1,000-m² lot. What percent of the rain ran off the ordinary asphalt lot?

mistakes.why: 1,000 m² is the area. Find the volume of rain first: 0.030 m × 1,000 m² = 30 m³.
10% is the share that did not run off. Runoff was 27 of 30 m³.

items.q: How much more does it cost to build a 1,000-m² lot with permeable pavers than with ordinary asphalt?

mistakes.why: 50 dollars is the extra cost for one square meter. Multiply by 1,000 m².
90,000 dollars is the whole cost of the paver lot. The question asks how much more: subtract 40,000.

items.q: A town has a small budget and wants the biggest cut in runoff for each extra dollar. Using the table, which design should it choose?
options: Asphalt draining to a rain garden
Permeable pavers
Porous asphalt
Ordinary asphalt with no change

why.correct: Runoff cut per extra dollar per m²: rain garden $\frac{15}{15} = 1.0$; porous asphalt $\frac{18}{30} = 0.6$; pavers $\frac{21}{50} = 0.42$.
options: Right: 15 m³ less runoff for 15 dollars more per m², the most cut per extra dollar.
Pavers cut 21 m³ for 50 dollars more per m²: the most in total, but the least per extra dollar.
Porous asphalt cuts 18 m³ for 30 dollars more per m², 0.6 m³ per extra dollar.
Ordinary asphalt does not reduce runoff at all.

items.q: Which are benefits of rain gardens in a city neighborhood? Select all that apply.
options: Less runoff reaches storm drains
Groundwater is recharged
Sediment and some pollutants are trapped by soil and plants
Rain is sent to the river faster
Lawns need more fertilizer
Streets get more flooding

why.correct: Rain gardens soak up runoff, recharge groundwater and filter water.
options: Right: runoff soaks in.
Right: water reaches groundwater.
Right: soil and roots trap material.
They slow water, not speed it.
Rain gardens do not need fertilizer; native plants are used.
They reduce street flooding.
